title: Living-wage policy is moving from voluntary corporate promise toward shared public-private wage infrastructure
source_unit: ILO news report on the first public-private partnerships under the Living Wage Programme, published 24 September 2026
geography: ILO member states and global supply chains; partnerships involve the Responsible Business Alliance, Unilever, and amfori across multiple countries and sourcing markets

observations.period: April 2025–September 2026; ILO Living Wage Programme partnership architecture

denominator.unit: first public-private partnership agreements signed under the ILO Living Wage Programme

partners.value: Responsible Business Alliance, Unilever, and amfori

policy_translation.value: the agreements translate a 2024 tripartite agreement on wage policies, including living wages, into country, sector, and company action

programme_launch.value: the agreements are the first of their kind since the Living Wage Programme launched in April 2025

observations.method: Official ILO account of partnership agreements and their stated objectives; it is a programme announcement, not evidence of wage changes or worker outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: The source does not specify countries, covered workers, wage baselines, implementation budgets, enforcement arrangements, or the time required to convert agreements into pay changes.
observations.subgroup: Workers and families in multinational supply chains, national wage-setting institutions, employers, worker organizations, governments, and consumers exposed to supply-chain labour conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Public-private agreements can harmonize methods without changing purchasing practices, prices, contracting power, or worker bargaining power; voluntary participation may leave the lowest-wage firms outside the architecture.

observations.period: 2026 onward; living-wage estimation and family-needs evidence

denominator.unit: ILO methodology and national-data route for living-wage estimation

needs_basis.value: estimates are intended to account for the needs of workers and their families, including the cost of a decent standard of living

economic_factors.value: relevant economic factors and national data are to inform estimates

institutional_alignment.value: initiatives are to align with ILO principles, the Minimum Wage Fixing Convention No. 131, and national wage-setting institutions

observations.method: ILO description of its living-wage estimation and operationalization approach.
observations.uncertainty: A common methodology does not settle local household baskets, care costs, housing, taxes, benefits, regional variation, inflation, or bargaining over who pays for wage increases.
observations.subgroup: Low-wage workers, dependents, households with care and housing costs, national statistical offices, wage boards, employers, unions, and sourcing communities.
observations.counterinterpretation: A quantified living-wage reference can improve comparability but can also become a technocratic ceiling, obscure household diversity, or be used by firms without corresponding collective bargaining and enforcement.

observations.period: 2026 onward; supply-chain scale and company-level roadmaps

denominator.unit: amfori member companies across more than 50 countries and sourcing markets

countries.unit: countries and sourcing markets, more than

unilever_route.value: ILO-convened roundtables and jointly developed roadmaps are intended to advance living wages at national, sectoral, and company levels in countries where Unilever operates

rba_route.value: RBA member companies will use ILO-grounded estimates and guidance to inform living-wage efforts in operations and supply chains

observations.method: ILO report of partner reach and intended supply-chain implementation mechanisms.
observations.uncertainty: Membership and roadmap reach do not establish worker coverage, wage increases, supplier compliance, purchasing-price changes, or whether benefits reach subcontracted and informal workers.
observations.subgroup: Workers in global supply chains, suppliers, subcontractors, multinational firms, sourcing communities, employers, unions, and consumers of branded goods.
observations.counterinterpretation: Large networks can spread a common method while concentrating agenda-setting in lead firms and associations; supplier cost pressure may be passed downward unless purchasing and bargaining conditions change.

denominator.unit: living-wage governance architecture connecting public, worker, employer, statistical, academic, and supply-chain actors

social_dialogue.value: governments, employers' organizations, and workers' organizations are named as primary drivers of change

data_partners.value: national statistical offices, academia, and research institutions are engaged to generate wage and economic data

collective_bargaining.value: operationalization is stated to respect national wage-setting institutions and collective bargaining autonomy

consumer_firm_link.value: wage-setting is linked to enterprise and economy sustainability and resilient supply chains

observations.method: ILO account of the programme's multi-actor architecture and stated safeguards.
observations.uncertainty: The architecture describes roles and principles but not actual bargaining power, representation quality, enforcement, dispute resolution, or consumer price and firm-profit effects.
observations.subgroup: Workers and families, trade unions, employers, public agencies, statistical institutions, firms, supply-chain actors, consumers, and communities producing traded goods.
observations.counterinterpretation: Stakeholder inclusion can remain consultative; collective-bargaining autonomy may be formally respected while lead-firm purchasing power and subcontracting still constrain negotiated outcomes.

ILO project page for estimating living wages in amfori member sourcing countries.

boundary: This record adds a wage-governance route linking household living costs, worker and family needs, national data, tripartite institutions, multinational supply chains, consumer-facing firms, and public-private standards. It is an announcement of agreements and intended mechanisms, not evidence of wage increases, worker welfare, bargaining power, price effects, or supply-chain compliance.
